data.boundaries#Boundaries:
go-gfx deliberately draws its edges:
Not image processing. Filters, edges, morphology, feature detection — that is go-images, the scikit-image analogue, which is built on raster / color / resample. Not a widget toolkit. Widgets, layout and event handling are go-widgets; its painter backend is built on vector / raster / color. Not text shaping. The text stack (fonts, shaping, glyph rasterization) is go-opentype; it stays separate and is composed alongside go-gfx, not inside it. Not 3D. The bespoke rasterizers in the game/virtio ports are deliberate C ports or 3D pipelines and are out of scope.
data.consumers#Consumers: Consumer Builds on Uses it for go-images raster, color, resample filters, edges, morphology, geometry go-widgets/painter vector, raster, color path fills, strokes, gradients go-webengine resample, codec, vector painting HTML/CSS layout to an image go-widgets/desktop codec, resample icon & thumbnail rendering
data.dependencies#Dependencies: go-gfx depends on nothing fleet-side at runtime. Its only optional dependency is go-asmgen, pulled in at code generation time to emit SIMD assembly for hot kernels; the committed library keeps a zero-dependency go.mod. The whole module cross-compiles to a static binary on all six of Go’s 64-bit targets.
data.why-a-foundation#Why a foundation:
2D graphics in most languages means binding a C engine — Skia, Cairo, Pixman. Across the Go fleet, several libraries had each grown their own copy of the same primitives:
an image processor resampling pixels, a widget toolkit rasterizing vector paths, a web engine decoding image codecs, a desktop stack rendering icons and thumbnails. That is duplicated, separately-tested, separately-buggy code. go-gfx extracts the shared substrate into one pure-Go, cgo-free module so colour blending, resampling, codecs and path rasterization are written and tested once.
It follows the classic layering — Skia / Cairo / image/draw: a foundation below, many renderers on top.
┌───────────────┐ ┌────────────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ consumers → │ go-images │ │ go-widgets/painter │ │ go-webengine │ … └───────┬───────┘ └─────────┬──────────┘ └──────┬───────┘ │ │ │ ┌───────┴───────────────────┴───────────────────┴───────┐ foundation → │ go-gfx/gfx │ │ geometry · color · raster · resample · codec · vector │ └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ ┌───────────┴───────────┐ optional SIMD → │ go-asmgen (gen-time) │ └───────────────────────┘

data.codec#codec:
One shared set of image decoders and encoders, so no consumer hand-rolls its own.
Decoders/encoders for PNG, JPEG, WebP, ICO, ICNS, GIF, TIFF. Subsumes the ad-hoc ICNS/ICO decoding the desktop stack used to carry, and the image loading go-webengine needs.
data.color#color:
Colour science done correctly, in linear light where it matters.
Colour models: RGB, XYZ, Lab, and conversions between them. sRGB ↔ linear transfer functions — so blends and resampling happen in linear light, not gamma-encoded space. Premultiplied alpha helpers, and Porter-Duff / separable blend modes. This is the package that keeps compositing and resampling from producing the dark-fringe artifacts that naive gamma-space math causes.
data.geometry#geometry:
Points, rectangles and affine transforms — the coordinate math every other layer shares.
Point, Rect value types with the usual predicates and set operations (union, intersection, containment). Affine 2×3 transform: translate, scale, rotate, shear, plus Concat / Invert and application to points and rectangles. Used pervasively: a resize is a scale transform, a codec crops with a Rect, a vector fill maps device space to user space through an Affine.
data.packages#Packages: go-gfx is a single Go module, github.com/go-gfx/gfx, split into focused packages. Import only what you need; each package is usable on its own and depends on nothing third-party.
data.raster#raster:
The shared pixel-buffer and pixel-format substrate — the common image surface every consumer reads and writes.
A concrete in-memory pixel buffer with an explicit pixel format. Format conversions between buffers (e.g. straight ↔ premultiplied, RGBA ↔ grayscale) built on color. raster is the hand-off type: go-images processes it, go-widgets/painter draws into it, go-webengine paints layout onto it.
data.resample#resample:
High-quality image resizing, separable and weight-precomputed.
Kernels: box / area averaging (downscale by coverage), bicubic (Catmull-Rom), and Lanczos. Separable implementation (horizontal pass into a scratch buffer, then vertical) with per-axis weights computed once. Validated against reference implementations and the naive 2-D definition. This is the first package landing in the module; go-images’ Resize and the desktop thumbnailer are the first consumers.
data.vector#vector:
The 2D vector engine renderers build on instead of rolling their own.
Paths: move/line/quad/cubic, with the usual builders. An anti-aliased scanline rasterizer (coverage-based). Strokes (width, joins, caps) and gradients (linear / radial). go-widgets/painter is the primary consumer; go-webengine paints CSS borders, backgrounds and shapes through it.

data.next-shared-codecs#Next — shared codecs: codec — PNG, JPEG, WebP, ICO, ICNS, GIF, TIFF, subsuming the hand-rolled ICNS/ICO decoding the desktop stack carries today. Wire go-images resize + the desktop thumbnailer onto resample.
data.now-bootstrapping#Now — bootstrapping:
Module skeleton — github.com/go-gfx/gfx, Go floor 1.26.4, BSD-3-Clause, the package boundary documented.
resample — the first landing package: box/area, bicubic (Catmull-Rom) and Lanczos, separable and weight-precomputed, validated against the naive 2-D definition and reference implementations.
raster + color (premultiplied alpha) — the pixel-buffer substrate and the colour math resample composites through.
webgpu — a second module, github.com/go-gfx/webgpu: WebGPU for Go in the browser, with batched encoding and surfaces. Released as v0.1.0. go-wasmcontainers/gpu runs on it; the go-quake1 renderer is the next consumer.
data.roadmap#Roadmap: go-gfx is a young foundation extracted from primitives that already existed, scattered, across the fleet. The plan is to land the substrate package by package, wiring each consumer over as its package stabilizes — incrementally, never big-bang (go-widgets/painter in particular is co-edited live and migrates one primitive at a time).
data.then-geometry-vector#Then — geometry \u0: geometry — points, rectangles, affine transforms. vector — paths, anti-aliased rasterizer, strokes, gradients — the engine go-widgets/painter hand-rolls today, migrated incrementally.
data.throughout-the-quality-bar#Throughout —: CGO_ENABLED=0 across the org; no Skia, no Cairo, no native shims. Zero third-party dependencies (go-asmgen only at generation time). 100% statement coverage, including error branches, gated in CI. Six architectures — build + test on amd64 / arm64 natively and loong64 / riscv64 / ppc64le / s390x under qemu. SIMD hot kernels via go-asmgen where they earn their keep, each validated bit-for-bit against a scalar oracle.

data.batched-encoding#Batched encoding:
A syscall/js call costs about 200 ns, ten times the WebGPU call it carries. A Recorder records a whole submit in Go and replays it with one call into replay.js, a plain same-origin script (it runs under script-src 'self'):
webgpu.InstallReplay(ctx, "/webgpu-replay.js") rec := device.NewRecorder() p := rec.BeginRenderPass(passDesc) p.SetPipeline(pipe) for _, s := range surfaces { p.SetBindGroup(0, s.group) p.DrawIndexed(s.count, 1, s.first, 0, 0) } p.End() seq, err := rec.Submit() err = device.WaitSubmitted(ctx, seq) Every command is checked as in the direct API. replay.js and its Go mirror read the same format with the same checks; the Go reader is fuzzed, and a browser test holds both to the same verdict on thousands of mutated streams. Submissions are numbered on a timeline (package timeline): completing one completes every earlier one, the fence model of virtio-gpu.
Measured on an Apple M4 Max, Chromium 143, Metal, CPU time per frame. The machine was loaded during these runs (1-minute load 10 to 16), so treat the numbers as indicative:
draws direct calls Recorder the same frame in JavaScript 1000 491 µs 85 µs 32 µs 5000 2320 µs 380 µs 138 µs That is about six times faster than direct calls, against the design’s estimate of fifteen. The estimate came from a prototype that recorded with no checks and no object table.
data.errors-at-the-call#Errors at the call: WebGPU reports most mistakes asynchronously, on the device. The package checks first and returns a *webgpu.BoundsError from the call: a write past a buffer, a texture region outside its mip level, a linear layout that does not fit its data (the specification’s “validating linear texture data”), a missing usage. The arithmetic is overflow checked, tested on 32-bit targets, and the copy check is fuzzed against an unbounded-integer oracle.
data.quotas#Quotas: A Quota bounds GPU memory (texture sizes are computed by the package), pipelines, WGSL size, surface size, and the optional features and limits a device may require (timestamp-query included). It is charged before the browser is called and refunded on Destroy, Release or device loss; the go-wasmcontainers playground gives one to each untrusted container.
data.surfaces#Surfaces: if err := webgpu.CanvasSupport(); err != nil { // errors.Is(err, webgpu.ErrNoCanvasContext): fall back to another renderer } s, err := device.NewSurface(webgpu.SurfaceDescriptor{Width: 640, Height: 480}) tex, err := s.CurrentTexture() bitmap, err := s.Present() // ImageBitmap, moved out without a copy MDN’s compatibility data lists the WebGPU context of OffscreenCanvas in Chrome 113 (every platform from 144), Safari 26, and Firefox 141 on Windows only. Elsewhere, CanvasSupport is the signal to fall back to another renderer.
data.tests#Tests: The platform-neutral code (descriptors, validation, quotas, the recorder) has every block covered on Linux, macOS, Windows and linux/386. The calls run in a real browser worker through go test -exec and Playwright. On macOS a GPU is required and a fallback adapter fails the run; Linux runs on SwiftShader. Every frame is checked pixel by pixel.
data.webgpu#WebGPU for Go in the browser:
github.com/go-gfx/webgpu is a typed Go API over the browser’s WebGPU, for any Go program built with GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm that runs in a window or a worker. It is the shared layer under the go-wasmcontainers GPU host (wasi:webgpu, wasi-nn) and the browser game renderers (go-quake1).
Released: v0.1.0. Install it with go get github.com/go-gfx/webgpu@v0.1.0. Before 1.0, a minor version may change the API. The go-wasmcontainers GPU host runs on this release. import "github.com/go-gfx/webgpu" g, err := webgpu.Navigator() // navigator.gpu a, err := g.RequestAdapter(ctx, nil) // refuses a fallback adapter by default d, err := a.RequestDevice(ctx, &webgpu.DeviceDescriptor{Quota: q}) b, err := d.CreateBuffer(webgpu.BufferDescriptor{Size: 64, Usage: webgpu.BufferUsageVertex | webgpu.BufferUsageCopyDst}) err = d.Queue().WriteBuffer(b, 0, vertices) // range checked at the call
data.what-it-covers#What it covers: Adapters and devices (device loss as a channel), buffers and mapping, textures of every format of the specification, views, samplers, WriteTexture for dirty rectangles, texture and buffer copies. Bind group and pipeline layouts, bind groups, render and compute pipelines (sync and async), depth-stencil, blending, multisampling. Render passes with indexed, instanced and indirect draws, render bundles, compute passes, error scopes, uncaptured errors. Surfaces: an OffscreenCanvas with a WebGPU context, frames out as ImageBitmaps.
